items.stem: Which property is shown by all metals?
items.answer: They conduct electricity when solid
items.markingKey: Metals have delocalised electrons, so they conduct as solids.

items.stem: Explain why metals are malleable.
items.answer: The layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonds, because the delocalised electrons hold the ions together.

items.stem: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals.
items.answer: Metals: good conductors, malleable/ductile, shiny, usually high m.p.; non-metals: poor conductors (except graphite), brittle when solid, dull, usually low m.p.

items.stem: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: calcium + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + hydrogen; Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂

items.stem: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute nitric acid. Include state symbols.
items.answer: magnesium + nitric acid → magnesium nitrate + hydrogen; Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: word equation [1]; formulae [1]; balancing [1]; state symbols [1]

items.stem: Ines adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — iron: slow fizzing; a pale green solution forms; zinc: steady fizzing; the metal slowly dissolves; magnesium: rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly and the tube gets warm. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of zinc with hydrochloric acid. (b) Suggest a metal that would show no reaction with the acid and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ (b) Copper (or silver/gold): it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

items.stem: Which word describes a metal that can be drawn out into wires?
items.answer: ductile
items.markingKey: Ductile = can be drawn into wires; malleable = can be hammered into shape.

items.stem: A piece of calcium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. What is observed?
options: rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly and the tube gets warm
very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly
slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing
items.answer: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly
items.markingKey: calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂

items.stem: Explain why magnesium ribbon is cleaned with sandpaper before it is reacted with acid.
items.answer: To remove the layer of magnesium oxide, so the metal itself reacts and the rate is not slowed.

items.stem: Describe a test to identify the gas formed when a metal reacts with a dilute acid.
items.answer: Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube: it burns with a squeaky pop (hydrogen).

items.stem: Explain why aluminium reacts slowly with dilute acid at first and then more quickly.
items.answer: A thin protective oxide layer must react/dissolve first; once the metal surface is exposed it reacts steadily.

items.stem: An unknown element E has these properties — electrical conductivity: poor (except graphite); appearance: dull; type of oxide: acidic. Deduce whether E is a metal or a non-metal, explaining your reasoning using each property.
items.answer: Non-metal: poor (except graphite) electrical conductivity is typical of a non-metal; dull appearance is typical of a non-metal; acidic type of oxide is typical of a non-metal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark per property correctly linked, max [3]

items.stem: An unknown element E has these properties — electrical conductivity: good; effect of hammering: malleable; appearance: shiny (lustrous). Deduce whether E is a metal or a non-metal, explaining your reasoning using each property.
items.answer: Metal: good electrical conductivity is typical of a metal; malleable effect of hammering is typical of a metal; shiny (lustrous) appearance is typical of a metal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark per property correctly linked, max [3]

items.stem: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced when 0.560 g of calcium reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid. Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂
items.answer: 336 cm³

items.stem: 1.20 g of magnesium is heated in air until it is completely converted to magnesium oxide, MgO. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of oxide formed and the increase in mass.
items.answer: 2.00 g; increase 0.800 g
items.markingKey: n = 1.20/24 = 0.0500 mol [1]; n(oxide) the same; mass = 0.0500 × 40 = 2.00 g [1]; increase = 0.800 g (mass of oxygen combined) [1]

items.stem: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced when 1.08 g of aluminium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂
items.answer: 1440 cm³

items.stem: 0.400 g of calcium is heated in air until it is completely converted to calcium oxide, CaO. 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO. Calculate the mass of oxide formed and the increase in mass.
items.answer: 0.560 g; increase 0.160 g
items.markingKey: n = 0.400/40 = 0.0100 mol [1]; n(oxide) the same; mass = 0.0100 × 56 = 0.560 g [1]; increase = 0.160 g (mass of oxygen combined) [1]

items.stem: Describe what is seen when iron is heated in oxygen, and write the balanced equation.
items.answer: Iron wool burns with orange sparks forming a dark solid; 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃
items.markingKey: 1 mark observation; 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced [3]

items.stem: Diego adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — zinc: steady fizzing; the metal slowly dissolves; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly; aluminium: slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing. (a) State two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test. (b) Predict what would be seen if aluminium powder were used instead of a piece.
items.answer: (a) Any two: size/mass/surface area of metal; volume, concentration and temperature of acid. (b) Faster fizzing (larger surface area) but the same total volume of gas for the same mass.

items.stem: Felix adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — copper: no reaction; zinc: steady fizzing; the metal slowly dissolves; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. (a) Put the three metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) Describe a test for the gas produced.
items.answer: (a) calcium > zinc > copper (b) Lighted splint — squeaky pop: hydrogen.

items.stem: Isla adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — zinc: steady fizzing; the metal slowly dissolves; aluminium: slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium with hydrochloric acid. (b) State two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test. (c) Predict what would be seen if calcium powder were used instead of a piece.
items.answer: (a) Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂ (b) Any two: size/mass/surface area of metal; volume, concentration and temperature of acid. (c) Faster fizzing (larger surface area) but the same total volume of gas for the same mass.

items.stem: What is an alloy?
options: A mixture of a metal with other elements
A pure metal that has been heated
items.answer: A mixture of a metal with other elements
items.markingKey: Alloys are mixtures (not compounds) of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals or carbon.

items.stem: Explain why an alloy is classified as a mixture and not a compound.
items.answer: The elements are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio; the composition can vary and the components keep their properties.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why pure copper is soft but brass is much harder.
items.answer: In pure copper all atoms are the same size in regular layers that slide easily; in brass the larger zinc atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide easily.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: pure metal layers slide; 1 mark: different-sized atoms disrupt layers [2]

items.stem: A 250 g key is made of bronze containing 9% tin by mass. Calculate the mass of tin and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 22.5 g tin; 228 g other

items.stem: Analysis of a solder object shows it contains 3.20 g of lead, which is 42% of the alloy by mass. Calculate the mass of the object and the mass of the other metal(s) in it.

An engineer compares duralumin with the pure metal aluminium for making aircraft bodies. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) A 80 g item contains 4% copper. Calculate the mass of copper. (c) Suggest why duralumin is suitable for aircraft bodies.
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) 3.20 g (c) Low density but much stronger than pure aluminium.

items.stem: Which metals are mixed to make brass?
items.answer: copper and zinc

items.stem: Describe the structure of an alloy as it would be shown in a diagram.
items.answer: A regular arrangement of metal atoms with some atoms of a different size dotted among them, distorting the layers.

items.stem: Explain why pure aluminium is not used for aircraft bodies but duralumin is.
items.answer: Pure aluminium is too soft/weak; duralumin keeps the low density but is much stronger.

items.stem: Explain why alloys still conduct electricity.
items.answer: They still contain metal atoms with delocalised electrons that can move through the structure.

items.stem: Brass (copper and zinc) is used for musical instruments, door handles and electrical plug pins. Explain why brass is chosen instead of pure copper.
items.answer: Brass is harder and more resistant to corrosion than pure copper; pure copper is softer/weaker. The atoms of different size in the alloy stop the layers sliding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property of alloy relevant to use; 1 mark: comparison with pure metal / structural reason [2]

items.stem: Solder (tin and lead (or tin with copper and silver)) is used for joining electrical components. Explain why solder is chosen instead of pure tin.
items.answer: Solder is low melting point; pure tin is less suitable. The atoms of different size in the alloy stop the layers sliding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property of alloy relevant to use; 1 mark: comparison with pure metal / structural reason [2]

items.stem: A 500 g sample of stainless steel contains 18% chromium by mass. What mass of chromium does it contain?
A 80 g key is made of solder containing 44% lead by mass. Calculate the mass of lead and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 35.2 g lead; 44.8 g other

items.stem: A 25 g key is made of solder containing 40% lead by mass. Calculate the mass of lead and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 10.0 g lead; 15.0 g other

items.stem: Lina is investigating why duralumin is used for aircraft bodies. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) Hardness values (arbitrary units): bronze 110; pure copper 45; duralumin 120. Which material is hardest and what does this suggest about alloys compared with pure metals?
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) duralumin; alloys are generally harder than the pure metals they contain.

items.stem: Analysis of a stainless steel object shows it contains 12.8 g of chromium, which is 15% of the alloy by mass. Calculate the mass of the object and the mass of the other metal(s) in it.

Isla is investigating why solder is used for joining electrical components. (a) Hardness values (arbitrary units): pure iron 70; bronze 110; stainless steel 200. Which material is hardest and what does this suggest about alloys compared with pure metals? (b) Explain why an alloy has no fixed melting point, unlike a pure metal.
items.answer: (a) stainless steel; alloys are generally harder than the pure metals they contain. (b) It is a mixture whose composition can vary, so it melts over a range of temperatures.

items.stem: A manufacturer in Dubai makes car bodies and machinery from mild steel, an alloy of iron and a small amount of carbon. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) Explain, using a description of the particles, why mild steel is harder than pure iron. (c) Hardness values (arbitrary units): stainless steel 200; pure tin 5; pure copper 45. Which material is hardest and what does this suggest about alloys compared with pure metals?
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) Atoms of different sizes distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily. (c) stainless steel; alloys are generally harder than the pure metals they contain.

items.stem: A manufacturer in Manila makes aircraft bodies from duralumin, an alloy of aluminium, copper and magnesium. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) A 120 g item contains 4% copper. Calculate the mass of copper. (c) Suggest why duralumin is suitable for aircraft bodies. (d) Explain why an alloy has no fixed melting point, unlike a pure metal.
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) 4.80 g (c) Low density but much stronger than pure aluminium. (d) It is a mixture whose composition can vary, so it melts over a range of temperatures.

items.stem: Why is aluminium used for overhead power cables rather than copper?
options: It has a lower density and is a good conductor
items.answer: It has a lower density and is a good conductor
items.markingKey: Al: low density so pylons can be further apart; it still conducts well (often with a steel core for strength).

items.stem: Which property of copper makes it suitable for electrical wiring?
options: It is a good conductor of electricity and is ductile
items.answer: It is a good conductor of electricity and is ductile
items.markingKey: Wires need high conductivity and ductility.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium is used for aircraft even though steel is stronger.
items.answer: Aluminium (alloy) has a much lower density, so the aircraft is lighter and uses less fuel, while still being strong enough; it also resists corrosion.

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for kitchen sinks and justify your choice. iron: density 7.87 g/cm³, conductivity 10 MS/m, corrosion — rusts, cost $0.5/kg; copper: density 8.96 g/cm³, conductivity 60 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $8.5/kg; aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm³, conductivity 38 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $2.4/kg; stainless steel: density 8.0 g/cm³, conductivity 1.4 MS/m, corrosion — does not rust, cost $3.0/kg.
items.answer: stainless steel: no rusting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice (stainless steel); 1 mark justification using data (no rusting); 1 mark comparison with another material [3]

items.stem: A company in Karachi is choosing a metal for manufacture of aircraft. (a) Data: aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; copper density 8.96 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; brass density 8.5 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion. Identify the least dense metal and suggest one use that benefits from its low density. (b) Other than physical properties, suggest one factor that affects the choice of metal.
items.answer: (a) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion). (b) Cost, availability, ease of recycling, appearance or toxicity.

items.stem: Why is aluminium used for food containers?
options: It reacts with acids in food
items.answer: It resists corrosion
items.markingKey: A thin oxide layer protects it; it is also non-toxic.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium resists corrosion even though it is a reactive metal.
items.answer: It is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that prevents air and water reaching the metal.

items.stem: Explain why copper is used for water pipes but iron is not.
items.answer: Copper does not react with water (it is unreactive), whereas iron rusts in water and air.

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for the hull of a lightweight boat and justify your choice. iron: density 7.87 g/cm³, conductivity 10 MS/m, corrosion — rusts, cost $0.5/kg; copper: density 8.96 g/cm³, conductivity 60 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $8.5/kg; zinc: density 7.14 g/cm³, conductivity 17 MS/m, corrosion — corrodes slowly, cost $2.8/kg; aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm³, conductivity 38 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $2.4/kg.
items.answer: aluminium: low density and corrosion resistance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice (aluminium); 1 mark justification using data (low density and corrosion resistance); 1 mark comparison with another material [3]

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for electrical wiring and justify your choice. zinc: density 7.14 g/cm³, conductivity 17 MS/m, corrosion — corrodes slowly, cost $2.8/kg; aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm³, conductivity 38 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $2.4/kg; stainless steel: density 8.0 g/cm³, conductivity 1.4 MS/m, corrosion — does not rust, cost $3.0/kg; copper: density 8.96 g/cm³, conductivity 60 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $8.5/kg.
items.answer: copper: highest electrical conductivity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice (copper); 1 mark justification using data (highest electrical conductivity); 1 mark comparison with another material [3]

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for overhead power cables and justify your choice. brass: density 8.5 g/cm³, conductivity 16 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $6.0/kg; aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm³, conductivity 38 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $2.4/kg; stainless steel: density 8.0 g/cm³, conductivity 1.4 MS/m, corrosion — does not rust, cost $3.0/kg; iron: density 7.87 g/cm³, conductivity 10 MS/m, corrosion — rusts, cost $0.5/kg.
items.answer: aluminium: high conductivity for its density.

items.answer: copper: highest electrical conductivity.

items.stem: Engineers are reviewing the materials used for food containers and drinks cans in a new factory. (a) Explain how this property relates to the structure of aluminium. (b) Data: brass density 8.5 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; copper density 8.96 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion. Identify the least dense metal and suggest one use that benefits from its low density.
items.answer: (a) Metallic structure: delocalised electrons give conductivity; layers of ions give malleability/ductility; oxide layer or alloying gives corrosion resistance. (b) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion).

items.stem: Kwame writes a report on why copper is used for saucepan bases. (a) State the property of copper that makes it suitable for saucepan bases. (b) Explain how this property relates to the structure of copper. (c) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion). (d) Cost, availability, ease of recycling, appearance or toxicity.

items.stem: Why is stainless steel used for cutlery?

It is soft and easily bent

items.stem: Stainless steel (iron, chromium, nickel and carbon) is used for cutlery, sinks, surgical instruments and chemical plant. Explain why stainless steel is chosen instead of pure iron.

items.stem: Yusuf adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — magnesium: rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly and the tube gets warm; iron: slow fizzing; a pale green solution forms; copper: no reaction. (a) Describe how the gas could be collected and its volume measured. (b) Explain why one of the metals shows no reaction.
items.answer: (a) Connect the tube to a gas syringe (or collect over water in an inverted measuring cylinder) and read the volume. (b) Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

items.stem: Lucas adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — aluminium: slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing; iron: slow fizzing; a pale green solution forms; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. (a) Describe how the gas could be collected and its volume measured. (b) Suggest a metal that would show no reaction with the acid and explain why. (c) Predict what would be seen if aluminium powder were used instead of a piece.
items.answer: (a) Connect the tube to a gas syringe (or collect over water in an inverted measuring cylinder) and read the volume. (b) Copper (or silver/gold): it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. (c) Faster fizzing (larger surface area) but the same total volume of gas for the same mass.

items.stem: Why are alloys usually harder than the pure metals they are made from?
options: Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily
The atoms in alloys are all the same size
items.answer: Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily
items.markingKey: Atoms of different size distort the regular lattice and stop layers sliding.

items.stem: Cupronickel (copper and nickel) is used for silver-coloured coins. Explain why cupronickel is chosen instead of pure copper.
items.answer: Cupronickel is hard, hard-wearing and resistant to corrosion; pure copper is softer/weaker. The atoms of different size in the alloy stop the layers sliding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property of alloy relevant to use; 1 mark: comparison with pure metal / structural reason [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why alloys still conduct electricity. (b) Explain why an alloy is classified as a mixture and not a compound.
items.answer: (a) They still contain metal atoms with delocalised electrons that can move through the structure. (b) The elements are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio; the composition can vary and the components keep their properties.

items.stem: A 200 g key is made of duralumin containing 4% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of copper and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 8.00 g copper; 192 g other

items.stem: A 150 g key is made of solder containing 37% lead by mass. Calculate the mass of lead and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 55.5 g lead; 94.5 g other

items.stem: An engineer compares solder with the pure metal tin for making joining electrical components. (a) A 80 g item contains 40% lead. Calculate the mass of lead. (b) Hardness values (arbitrary units): pure tin 5; stainless steel 200; pure copper 45. Which material is hardest and what does this suggest about alloys compared with pure metals?
items.answer: (a) 32.0 g (b) stainless steel; alloys are generally harder than the pure metals they contain.

items.stem: An engineer compares bronze with the pure metal copper for making statues, medals and ship propellers. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) Explain, using a description of the particles, why bronze is harder than pure copper. (c) Hardness values (arbitrary units): pure tin 5; duralumin 120; bronze 110. Which material is hardest and what does this suggest about alloys compared with pure metals?
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) Atoms of different sizes distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily. (c) duralumin; alloys are generally harder than the pure metals they contain.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which property of copper makes it suitable for electrical wiring? (b) Give one use of brass.
items.answer: (a) It is a good conductor of electricity and is ductile (b) Musical instruments, door handles, electrical plug pins or ornaments.
items.markingKey: (a) Wires need high conductivity and ductility. (b) [1]

items.stem: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables.
items.answer: Because of its low density and good electrical conductivity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark property; 1 mark linked to the use [2]

items.stem: Explain why brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings.
items.answer: Because of its hardness, attractive colour and resistance to corrosion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark property; 1 mark linked to the use [2]

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for the hull of a lightweight boat and justify your choice. zinc: density 7.14 g/cm³, conductivity 17 MS/m, corrosion — corrodes slowly, cost $2.8/kg; brass: density 8.5 g/cm³, conductivity 16 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $6.0/kg; aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm³, conductivity 38 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $2.4/kg; stainless steel: density 8.0 g/cm³, conductivity 1.4 MS/m, corrosion — does not rust, cost $3.0/kg.
items.answer: aluminium: low density and corrosion resistance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice (aluminium); 1 mark justification using data (low density and corrosion resistance); 1 mark comparison with another material [3]

items.stem: A company in Madrid is choosing a metal for cutlery. (a) State the property of stainless steel that makes it suitable for cutlery. (b) Explain how this property relates to the structure of stainless steel. (c) Other than physical properties, suggest one factor that affects the choice of metal.
items.answer: (a) hardness and resistance to rusting (b) Metallic structure: delocalised electrons give conductivity; layers of ions give malleability/ductility; oxide layer or alloying gives corrosion resistance. (c) Cost, availability, ease of recycling, appearance or toxicity.
